opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it goes back to how I came into the field. A lot of my early work, at DeepMind on things like reinforcement learning agents and games, was essentially built on synthetic data. When you train an agent in a simulated environment, every single experience it learns from is generated. There's no human-labeled dataset sitting underneath it. And what you see, again and again, is that if you can build the right generator, the right environment, you can get effectively unlimited data, and you can shape that data to teach exactly what you want the model to learn.

So for me synthetic data isn't some exotic trick. It's the natural way to scale learning once you hit the limits of what exists in the world. And in a lot of domains we hit those limits very quickly. In drug discovery, for example, which is what I spend my time on now, experimental data is incredibly expensive and slow to collect. You might have a few hundred thousand protein structures that took decades of painstaking lab work to resolve. That's tiny compared to what modern models can absorb.

What gets me excited is that you can use models themselves, along with physics-based tools and known constraints, to generate new, high-quality training examples. Then you train on those, the model gets better, and you can generate even better data. That flywheel is really powerful. We saw versions of it with self-play in games, with distillation in structure prediction, and I think it's going to be central to how we build models that understand biology and chemistry at a level real-world data alone could never get us to.

The key, of course, is that it's not free. Synthetic data is only as good as your ability to verify it and to keep it grounded in reality. You need a way to filter, to check, to make sure you aren't just amplifying the model's own mistakes. But when you get that loop right, it lets you go well beyond the data you happen to have. That's why I'm such a believer.

r001.rationale: It says synthetic data can extend limited, expensive real-world data, but does not identify it as a way for researchers to offset large organizations’ data advantage.

r002.rationale: It mentions physics-based tools and known constraints for generating examples, but does not identify physical-theory-grounded simulation as the source.

r003.rationale: It discusses filtering and checking generated examples, but does not state that scoring systems applied to generative-model outputs enhance their information content.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think it comes down to a fairly simple observation: for most of the problems I actually care about, the data you'd want to learn from doesn't exist yet. It's not sitting on the internet waiting to be scraped. If you want a system that reasons about biology, or plays a game at a superhuman level, or acts in the world over long horizons, the trajectories that demonstrate that capability have to be generated, because no human has ever produced them.

The thing that really convinced me was watching what happened with self-play in reinforcement learning. In AlphaStar, the agents weren't learning from human replays past a certain point. They were generating their own curriculum by playing each other, and the data they produced was, in a very real sense, synthetic. It was far more valuable than anything we could have collected from people, because it was targeted at exactly the weaknesses the agents had at that moment. That's the key property for me. Synthetic data isn't just more data, it's data you can aim.

The second reason is control. When you rely on naturally occurring data, you inherit all of its biases, its gaps, its noise, and you have very little visibility into what's actually in there. When you generate it, you know the generating process. You can vary it systematically, you can hold out things cleanly, you can ask counterfactual questions. In a scientific setting that matters enormously, because the whole point is to learn something about the world rather than to memorise a dataset.

And the third reason is that we're clearly hitting the limits of the "just scrape more" approach. The static corpus of human text is finite and we've largely consumed it. So the question isn't whether synthetic data will matter, it's how we make the loop between model and simulator, or model and experiment, or model and verifier, tight enough that the generated data keeps improving the model rather than just reflecting its existing mistakes back at it. That's where I think most of the interesting research is right now.

r001.rationale: The response discusses generating targeted data when useful examples do not exist, but does not connect this to limited-data researchers compensating for large organizations’ data advantage.

r002.rationale: It mentions simulators generally, but does not identify simulation grounded in physical theory as a source of synthetic chemistry data.

r003.rationale: It does not describe applying scoring systems to generative-model data or enhancing that data’s information content.

astra-6.text:
I think the exciting thing about synthetic data is that it lets you move beyond the data you happen to have collected. You can generate examples that target exactly what a model needs to learn, control their difficulty, and often get the correct labels essentially for free.

Think about a system learning by playing a game. Every time it plays, it generates new experience. As it improves, it can encounter harder challenges, so the data evolves alongside the model. That creates a really powerful learning loop.

The caveat is that generating more data isn’t automatically useful. If your generator has blind spots, you can reinforce those. You need to check that what the model learns actually transfers to the task you care about. But when you get that loop right, synthetic data gives you a way to scale learning beyond a fixed dataset.

sol-6.1.text:
The exciting thing about synthetic data is that you can turn data generation into something you control. You can generate examples, get the labels automatically, and deliberately vary the things you want a model to understand. That gives you a way to explore situations that might be rare or difficult to capture in real data.

But I wouldn’t say synthetic data is automatically useful. The question is whether learning from it helps with the task you actually care about. You can generate enormous quantities of data and still miss something important. What makes it powerful is that you can test that, change the generator, and improve the training distribution. So you’re designing the learning experience, as well as designing the model.
